text:
🛑 LEGAL NOTICE 

To,

Mr. Markandey Katju
Former Judge, Supreme Court of India
X Handle:@mkatju,

Subject: Legal Notice for Immediate Removal of Blasphemous Post, Public Apology, and Cessation of Further Acts Outraging Hindu Religious Sentiments, Failing Which Legal Proceedings Shall Be Initiated.

Sir,

1. You have, on 25 April 2026 at 11:23 PM, posted on your verified X account (@mkatju) a highly offensive, derogatory, and blasphemous digital image. The image deliberately superimposes the face of Mr. Donald Trump upon the sacred form of Bhagwan Vishnu, complete with blue skin, Sheshnag, peacock feather crown, Shankha, Chakra, Lotus, Gada and other divine attributes. A screenshot of the said post is annexed for your reference.

2. Despite seeing massive public outrage and strong condemnation from thousands of users on X and across social media, instead of deleting the offending post, you have posted the same post/image again. This clearly confirms your deliberate and malicious intent to insult and outrage the religious feelings of Hindus.

3. This act constitutes a deliberate and malicious insult to the religious beliefs and sentiments of crores of Hindus who revere Bhagwan Vishnu as a Supreme Deity of Sanatan Dharma. Your post is not an exercise of legitimate satire or freedom of expression but a calculated attempt to mock and denigrate Hindu faith.

4. As a retired Judge of the Supreme Court of India, you are expected to maintain the highest standards of judicial dignity, constitutional morality and respect for the religious feelings of citizens. Instead, you have repeatedly misused your platform to hurt Hindu sentiments.

5. The said post has caused widespread public outrage across the country. Thousands of citizens have strongly condemned your act on social media. Despite this massive backlash, you have shown complete indifference to the hurt and anguish caused to the Hindu community.

6. Your actions squarely attract the offences punishable under:  
- Section 299 BNS (Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings)  
- Section 199 BNS (Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion)  
- Section 197 & 353 BNS and other relevant provisions  
Read with provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

7. You are hereby called upon to take note of the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s binding Order dated 28.04.2023 passed in Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay vs. Union of India (W.P.(C) No.943/2021), wherein the Apex Court has directed all States/UTs to register suo moto FIRs against acts that outrage religious feelings under Sections 153A, 153B, 295A, 505 IPC etc., without waiting for any formal complaint, irrespective of the religion or status of the offender. Failure to act by authorities shall amount to contempt of the Supreme Court.

DEMANDS:
 
You are hereby directed to:
a) Immediately delete the offending posts and all similar posts from your X account and all other digital platforms within 24 hours of receipt/notice of this Legal Notice.
b) Issue a public unconditional apology on your X handle @mkatju for hurting the religious sentiments of Hindus.
c) Undertake in writing that you shall refrain from any further acts of blasphemy or hurting religious sentiments of any community.

Please Take notice that in case you fail to comply with the above demands within the stipulated time, I shall be constrained to:

* Initiate appropriate criminal proceedings against you before the competent Court of law;

* File complaints before the Police for registration of FIR as per the Supreme Court directions; and

* Take all other legal remedies available to me under the law, including civil suit for damages.

This notice is sent to you without prejudice to my rights and contentions.  

Amita Sachdeva
Advocate-on-Record
Supreme Court of India

Note: I have attached herewith two screenshots of comments by X users showing the widespread outrage and hurt caused by your post.

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.

One Blocking Order Every 68 Seconds: When the State Starts Controlling the Digital Public Square

[The News Minute — 1.95 lakh blocking orders in five months]
https://t.co/4pKxvmx3EL

The number is staggering:

Nearly 1.95 lakh government blocking directions to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026 — roughly one every 68 seconds. 

And there is an important caveat: 1.95 lakh blocking orders do not necessarily mean 1.95 lakh individual posts were removed. A single order can cover hundreds of posts, accounts or pieces of content. 

But even with that qualification, the scale demands serious democratic scrutiny.

The distribution is striking:

Instagram: nearly 1 lakh orders

Facebook: around 80,000

YouTube: nearly 15,000

Most were routed through the Union Home Ministry's Sahyog portal. Meta has also integrated its systems with the portal, allowing flagged material to be removed automatically in response to government directions. 

And the timing cannot simply be ignored.

These five months overlapped with the student protests over examination irregularities, during which social media became an important tool for mobilisation and public discussion. Reporting has also documented takedowns involving posts supporting the protests and criticism of government policies. 

There is another crucial legal distinction that must not be lost in the political debate:

These 1.95 lakh directions should not all be described as Section 69A blocking orders. A significant proportion were issued through Sahyog under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, which operates differently from Section 69A. 

That distinction makes the central democratic question even more important:

Who decides what citizens are allowed to see, question and share — and what independent mechanism exists to challenge that decision?

A democratic government unquestionably needs mechanisms to tackle deepfakes, fraud, cybercrime, incitement and genuinely unlawful content.

But those powers must come with transparency, due process, accountability and meaningful avenues of appeal.

Because social media is no longer merely entertainment.

It is where citizens organise, protest, educate one another, expose wrongdoing, criticise governments and participate in democracy.

When the machinery capable of silencing digital speech operates at the rate of one government blocking direction every 68 seconds, every citizen should be asking:

What is being blocked?
Why is it being blocked?
Who ordered it?
And who watches the people doing the blocking?

A democracy should never fear citizens who question power.

It should fear a system in which citizens become afraid to question it.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

🛜 🌍 The world's biggest domain seller GoDaddy says India's fight against fake websites could make the internet less safe. A fight not many are watching,  but is set to reshape internet governance, we report at @Reuters 

🌍Let's understand the background -- India has a fake-website problem. For years, fraudsters have registered domains impersonating global brands -- bogus Amazon shopping sites, fake McDonald's franchise offers, phony Microsoft support pages -- to con ordinary people. Dozens of companies took them to court.

🌍 What happened in December 2025? a Delhi judge cracked down. She blocked more than 1,100 fraudulent sites. But she didn't stop there.

She wrote sweeping new rules for the entire domain industry: strip away privacy protection by default, hand over website owners' details within 72 hours to anyone claiming a "legitimate interest," and block any web address resembling a protected brand.

🌍 The big news now: Now GoDaddy -- which runs 80 million domains worldwide -- is fighting back in thousands of pages of court filings my colleagues and I reviewed . Its warning is striking: the rules would make the internet less safe, not more. They'd expose ordinary website owners to stalking and harassment. And because domain systems are global, an order from one Delhi courtroom could ripple across the entire web -- potentially forcing GoDaddy to "exit India" altogether.

🌍 They are colourful filings: One of GoDaddy's arguments? That you can't ban the word "McDonald" -- it's a Scottish surname meaning "son of the world ruler."  The U.S. giant also submitted research compiled from the Merriam-Webster's website to argue that safeguarding variations of a protected trademark like "HUL" - Unilever's Indian unit, could overlap with 118 English words that contain the string, like "hulk" and "moghul".

🌍 It's a landmark collision between a nation trying to protect its citizens and the borderless architecture of the internet itself.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

The Joke That Is CJP

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

“Scanner de dijiye.”
“UPI kar deta hoon.”

These have become some of the most ordinary sentences in Indian life. That ordinariness is the achievement. Successful infrastructure is not technology displayed as spectacle; it is technology absorbed into everyday life and trusted without a second thought.

Exactly ten years ago, UPI was rolled out. India did not merely introduce another way to pay, it began transforming the relationship between citizens, commerce and money.

As a Chartered Accountant, I tend to trust numbers more than adjectives. In FY 2016–17, UPI processed approximately 1.8 crore transactions worth about ₹0.07 lakh crore. By FY 2025–26, that had risen to 24,161 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore.

In July 2026 alone, UPI processed 2,365 crore transactions worth ₹29.88 lakh crore: an average of approximately 76.3 crore transactions every day.

These figures tell us how far UPI has travelled.

UPI’s real achievement is that it made sophisticated financial infrastructure almost invisible. The same interoperable payments rail now serves a street vendor and a large retailer. A small entrepreneur receives money instantly. A family can transfer funds across the country in seconds. A student in a hostel can receive ₹500 from home before the phone call ends.

By June 2026, UPI had onboarded 55.49 crore users. The Government has also reported that it serves 6.5 crore merchants, while 741 banks were live on the platform by July. During FY 2025–26, UPI accounted for nearly 86% of India’s retail payment transactions by volume. An IMF Fintech Note describes it as the world’s largest retail fast payment system by volume.

Under Prime Minister @narendramodi Ji’s Digital India vision, India did not merely catch up with the digital revolution. We showed the world how technology could be built at population scale, made interoperable and delivered to the last mile.

#10YearsOfUPI is therefore not merely a celebration of an app. It is a celebration of public digital infrastructure, institutional trust and inclusion by design. 🇮🇳

The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), a bipartisan U.S. government body, has urged Washington to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials allegedly involved in religious-freedom violations, including revoking RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's U.S. visa.

This is not a U.S. ban on the RSS. USCIRF makes policy recommendations; the U.S. government has not announced such sanctions. However, the recommendation is significant: USCIRF's 2026 annual report had already recommended sanctions against the RSS, including asset freezes and entry restrictions.

COMMENTARY

There is an important distinction between “America has banned the RSS” and “a U.S. government commission is calling for sanctions against RSS members.”

Facts matter—especially when we are discussing something as serious as religious freedom.

But the factual correction should not make us miss the significance of what has actually happened.

A U.S. federal commission responsible for monitoring religious freedom has publicly placed the RSS within a framework of concern over alleged violations affecting religious minorities and is asking the U.S. government to consider punitive measures.

That is not a ban.

But it is not a trivial warning either.

For India, this should prompt something more meaningful than nationalist outrage.

If the allegations are false, answer them with evidence.

If they are exaggerated, demonstrate why.

If there are genuine failures in protecting minorities, investigate them honestly and correct them.

A confident democracy should never fear scrutiny.

And this issue should not be reduced to Hinduism versus America, or India versus the West.

The RSS is not Hinduism.

Criticism of a political ideology is not criticism of every Hindu.

And defending religious freedom is not an attack on any religion.

The real question is much larger:

Can a modern democracy allow any religious or political ideology to become so powerful that minorities begin to fear that citizenship itself has different meanings for different communities?

That is the question India must answer—not merely for Washington, not for the UN, and not for international observers.

For ourselves.

Because India's constitutional promise is not that one community will dominate another.

It is that every citizen will belong equally.

The world may criticise India.

The government may reject that criticism.

But neither reaction changes the underlying moral responsibility:

Protect the citizen. Protect equality. Protect freedom of conscience.

And if power is confident that it has done so, it should have no reason to fear an honest examination of the evidence.

THE REAL TAKEAWAY

No, the USA has not banned the RSS.

Yes, a U.S. government commission has called for targeted sanctions against RSS members and others.

Let's not exaggerate the first.

And let's not minimise the second.

— Reflection: A democracy does not become stronger by silencing uncomfortable questions. It becomes stronger when it has the courage to answer them.

CREDIT

Credit to Reuters for reporting the USCIRF recommendation and the responses surrounding Mohan Bhagwat's U.S. visit.

text:
Catastrophic flash flood on the Nepal–Tibet border (Wednesday, 26 August 2026). A glacial collapse sent a wall of mud, rock, ice and water down the Bhote Koshi / Lhende Khola into the Trishuli river system, wiping out villages, a border crossing, roads, bridges and hydropower plants. It is one of Nepal’s deadliest disasters in years.

WHAT EXACTLY HAPPENED:

Around 8:40 a.m. local time, a sudden surge of debris-laden water tore through Rasuwa district (north of Kathmandu) near the Rasuwagadhi / Gyirong Port crossing, then raced downstream through Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and other districts. Entire settlements and markets were buried or swept away. Videos from the Chinese side show people fleeing as a wall of mud hit the border post.

The USGS initially flagged a magnitude-4.4 earthquake but later determined there was no earthquake. The seismic signal came from the glacial collapse and debris flow itself. Satellite imagery points to an ice-and-rock landslide on the Tibetan side that temporarily dammed the river before the dam burst. Experts have warned of a possible second surge from remaining blocked water upstream.

Casualties (as of Thursday 27 August — still rising)
Confirmed dead: at least 165 (Nepal police recovered ~157–162 bodies; China reports 3 dead in Gyirong). Officials expect the toll to climb as searches continue.

MISSING: 

nearly 1,500 people across both countries.
-Nepal: ~826 unaccounted for (including ~500 foreigners / hundreds of tourists).
-Tibet (Gyirong county): 558 missing, including 260 foreigners.

Foreign nationals reported missing (figures vary slightly by source and are being updated):
-India: 142–177 (many Kailash–Mansarovar pilgrims)
-United States: 47–63
-Australia: 34
-United Kingdom: 33
-Canada: 24–25
Also: South Koreans (hydropower workers), Malaysians, and others from more than two dozen countries.

Locals, 28 Nepalese police, soldiers, customs staff and hydropower workers are also among the missing.

DAMAGES:

-19 bridges and ~40 km of road destroyed.
-Multiple hydropower plants hit (hundreds of MW offline  a significant share of Nepal’s capacity).
-Border infrastructure and villages in Rasuwa and Nuwakot heavily damaged. Mud is metres deep in places.

Today I am writing about a woman who was forced into marriage as a child.

Her husband is a drug addict, and they have a nine year old daughter. For years, it was this mother who kept her daughter fed, sheltered, and cared for by working in other people’s homes, washing dishes, clothes, and carpets just to make ends meet. Every now and then, her addicted husband would come home, beat his wife and daughter, and force them to find money to pay for his drugs.

Eventually, this woman managed to escape that horrific marriage. But today, a Taliban court ruled that, under Islamic Sharia, custody of the girl should go to this man simply because he is her father.

The mother completely broke down. She was crying and pleading in a way I have rarely witnessed. Through her tears, she kept screaming that this drug addict would take her daughter away, sell her during the day, and spend the money on drugs.

The little girl was scratching at her own face and pulling at her hair in sheer desperation. She kept saying, “I’m not going with this man.” But the Taliban had already given their order. In the end, they dragged her into a vehicle and took her away, while her devastated mother collapsed unconscious on the ground and had to be taken to the hospital.

This is what the harsh application of Islamic Sharia looks like under the Taliban, and what happens when justice is placed in the hands of a deeply broken system.

text:
Wednesday morning headlines from #Armenia, 26 August

● Former President Robert Kocharyan and his elder son, Sedrak Kocharyan, have been detained. Anti-Corruption Committee officers searched Kocharyan’s home, the home of his other son, Levon Kocharyan, an MP from the opposition pro-Russian Armenia bloc, and dozens of other addresses linked to the family. The former president’s office called the developments “another attack by the authorities against President Kocharyan.”

● The prosecutor initiated public criminal proceedings against Robert Kocharyan on charges of abuse of official powers (three counts), accepting a particularly large bribe (two counts) and large-scale money laundering (four counts). Criminal proceedings were also initiated against nine other people, including Sedrak Kocharyan, the former defense minister, a former prime minister, a former Yerevan mayor and an employee of Local Developers. The director of the former president’s mansion complex, who managed construction activities for the company Aigedzor, his wife and two daughters were also detained.

● The Anti-Corruption Court has received requests to remand six people in custody, including Sedrak Kocharyan.

● Levon Kocharyan’s lawyers said the search of his apartment was illegal because he has parliamentary immunity. They said security officers took commemorative medals from the apartment that were inscribed as wedding gifts. His minor children were at home and were frightened, his lawyer said.

● Levon Kocharyan called the criminal case against members of his family politically motivated and said that “no one in the family, including the children, is afraid of these masked raids.” “There is nothing new in this case. Since 2018 [when Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and his team came to power — JAMnews], the case has already been brought before the courts several times for various reasons. Nothing new has happened and nothing new has been uncovered,” the MP said.

● Anna Grigoryan, an MP from the same Armenia parliamentary faction, said “all of this is being done exclusively against the backdrop of upcoming concessions to Azerbaijan — the transfer of the village of Tigranashen and the adoption of an ‘Aliyev Constitution.’” “This is an attempt to neutralize the main players and create such an atmosphere of fear that no Armenian citizen with opposition views will dare to express their position. That is the main goal,” Grigoryan said.

Context: Armenia’s pro-Russian opposition has criticized the authorities over the ongoing process of constitutional amendments. The focus is on Armenia’s 1990 Declaration of Independence, which is referenced in the current Constitution. The declaration calls for the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. Azerbaijan considers this a territorial claim and insists that a peace agreement can be signed only after the provision is removed from Armenia’s Constitution. Armenian authorities have repeatedly said that constitutional changes are needed by Armenia itself and that the issue has never been discussed with anyone outside the country. A draft of the new Constitution is expected to be published in the coming weeks for nationwide public discussion.

● Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan commented on the arrests in social media posts. “Yes, Gagik Tsarukyan [an arrested businessman and pro-Russian politician] and Robert Kocharyan should both go to prison. They should be deprived of the money they can use to bribe people. This is my political responsibility, and the state cannot fail to do this. It’s not me saying this — it’s the Armenian people. The era of the mafia is over,” Pashinyan said.

● The European Court of Human Rights has accepted for consideration two complaints filed on behalf of Gagik Tsarukyan. His lawyers said his arrest was “illegal and politically motivated.”

● “Armenia will not prevent Russians who want to avoid mobilization and being sent to the front from entering the country,” Security Council Secretary Armen Grigoryan said in an interview with the Russian-language TV channel Dozhd. “No one at the border is going to ask anyone why they came here. Russian citizens can enter Armenia without a passport; an identity card is sufficient. I can tell Russians only one thing: ‘Welcome to Armenia.’ We love and respect everyone here,” Grigoryan said.

● Nikol Pashinyan also commented on the “March 1 case” — the deadly crackdown on a large protest in Yerevan on March 1, 2008, when demonstrators disputed the results of the presidential election. Firearms were used and 10 people were killed. Robert Kocharyan was president at the time and is the main defendant in the case. “Some people say the March 1 case has still not been solved. It has been solved, but the justice system, because of mafia influence from within, is not giving it a proper assessment. Obviously, the order to kill was given by Robert Kocharyan. But Armenia’s judicial and legal system is independent of the government, and it turns out that it can receive as much money as it wants from former oligarchs while delaying the examination of cases brought against them,” Pashinyan said.

● “Armenia is closer to the European Union than ever,” European Commission spokesperson Markus Lammert said at a briefing. “The first EU-Armenia summit in Yerevan was successful. There is positive cooperation under the Resilience and Growth Plan, the European Peace Facility and partnership missions. Yerevan has already taken the first step toward the EU by adopting a bill to launch the accession process, and this is an important symbolic step.”

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India Orders Immediate Takedown of Dhruv Rathee’s (@dhruv_rathee)  Video.

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, Government of India, has passed an Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) directing YouTube to remove the video titled “Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed” within 24 hours of receiving the Order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it has been uploaded today (19 July 2026).

Key points from the GAC Order:

- The video contains deliberate and malicious statements insulting Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.

- It falsely claims they consumed meat (including deer meat) and alcohol, using distorted references from scriptures.

- Such content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is against societal harmony.

- YouTube’s arguments on “free speech” were not accepted. Freedom of expression comes with reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order was issued after Hon'ble Delhi High Court’s direction on 3rd July 2026 to decide the appeal within 15 days.

Important: This observation and finding by the GAC that the video hurts religious sentiments will also have a strong bearing on the decision of the Ld. Magistrate before whom our petition seeking registration of FIR against Dhruv Rathee is pending for hearing on 10.09.2026.

Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of “content creation.” Justice is being delivered step by step.
Jai Shri Ram 🙏

A special thanks to Sr. Adv. Makarand D. Adkar Ji (@AdkarMakarand) for his invaluable guidance and support, and to our legal team for their tireless efforts and unwavering commitment.

Delay by Customs in re-assessing Bills of Entry and generating correct IGST challans: Bombay High Court directs Department to complete time-bound re-assessment within eight weeks with interim protection from coercive action.

Issue:
Whether the Department could be directed under writ jurisdiction to carry out re-assessment of six Bills of Entry, issue correct Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) payable challans, and grant an upfront waiver of statutory interest.

Rule:
Under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, re-assessment of imported goods and determination of applicable duty/tax liability must be conducted by the proper officer in accordance with binding judicial precedents laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Courts. Ancillary statutory levies such as interest fall within the realm of administrative adjudication during the re-assessment proceeding itself.

Application:
The Assessee approached the High Court invoking writ jurisdiction against the Department’s inaction in re-assessing six subject Bills of Entry, generating accurate IGST challans, and seeking relief against levy of interest. The Department fairly conceded to conducting the re-assessment exercise in a time-bound manner, while requesting that the claim for waiver of interest be left open for the proper officer's statutory determination. Adopting this consensus, the Court held that the re-assessment must be finalized in terms of established legal principles without the High Court delving prematurely into the merits or interest waiver.

Conclusion:
The High Court directed the Department to complete the re-assessment of the six Bills of Entry within eight weeks from the date of receipt of the certified copy of the order. While leaving the issue of interest waiver open for the proper officer to decide, the Court granted interim protection to the Assessee, directing that no coercive recovery action be initiated until the re-assessment exercise is completed.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling prevents arbitrary departmental inaction on customs re-assessments and protects importers from coercive recovery during pending adjudication, while reaffirming that statutory claims like interest waiver must first be examined by the adjudicating officer.

Department attempts to penalise an Independent Director under GST Section 122(1A); Bombay High Court steps in to grant interim protection against coercive recovery.

Issue:
Whether an individual serving as an Independent Director of a company comes within the scope of penalty provisions under Section 122(1A) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, and whether interim protection against coercive recovery is warranted.

Rule:
Section 122(1A) of the CGST Act, 2017 prescribes penal liability only on any person who retains the benefit of specified fraudulent transactions or at whose instance such transactions are conducted; as judicially interpreted by the Coordinate Bench in Shantanu Sanjay Hundekari, an individual acting in a non-beneficiary or official capacity does not automatically fall under the sweep of this section.

Application:
The Assessee was subjected to penalty proceedings under Section 122(1A) in an individual capacity while serving merely as an Independent Director of the company. The Assessee contended that he was not the company itself nor did he fall within the ambit of the penal provision, relying upon the Coordinate Bench ruling which had attained finality as the Supreme Court did not interfere with it. Upon examining the statutory provision and binding precedent, the High Court observed that a strong prima facie case was established in favour of the Assessee.

Conclusion:
Since a strong prima facie case was made out by the Assessee based on established judicial precedent, the High Court granted ad-interim relief and directed the Department not to take any coercive action regarding the penalty in question until further orders.

Impact Analysis:
This order reaffirms that the Department cannot routinely invoke Section 122(1A) against independent directors or corporate professionals in their individual capacities, offering vital interim immunity from coercive tax recovery where no direct personal involvement or retention of illicit benefit is established.

A Letter of Continuing Guarantee was created bearing a forged version of my signature. My PAN was mapped to a company-controlled email address on the NeSL statutory portal — a fabrication the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) confirmed to me in writing on 13.01.2026.

When I objected in writing, a second bank issued the takeover NOC anyway — later admitting in writing that it did so "due to repeated reminders from HDFC Bank."

One falsehood. Four institutions.

To the Central Crime Branch, Chennai: no document bears her signature. → Closure report, 07.02.2024.

To the Madras High Court: same. → Favourable order, 31.01.2025.

To the Reserve Bank of India: a different loan-application date than it filed in court. A different Board Resolution than it filed in court. And in July 2025 — "not a guarantor" — while the guarantee naming me sat in its own custody. → My complaint closed.

Then, in July 2026, two days before my RBI appeal hearing, HDFC produced that very Letter of Continuing Guarantee.

By its own hand, it proved every one of those statements false.

Section 46 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 makes furnishing wilfully false information to the RBI a punishable offence.

100+ complaints. Not one document ever verified.

Since 2023 my family has filed over 100 complaints — police, RBI, CPGRAMS, DPG, National Consumer Helpline, courts.

RBI's own Complaint Management System records 15 against HDFC and connected entities. First one: 12.06.2024.

Every single one closed.

Every closure based on the bank's own response — which no authority ever checked against a single document.

In three years, across a hundred complaints, not one authority asked HDFC to produce the guarantee it claimed to hold. The one document that would have ended this at the start.

And it kept lending

HDFC's own NeSL filings show money continued to move after my written fraud alert of 09.08.2023 — including a fresh cash credit of ₹5,49,91,000 on 17.09.2025.

The same filings record: "No authentication done by any parties till now."

What it cost

On 02.08.2026 my father — Shri Suresh Kumar K.A., 68, an accountant who stood beside me for three years, who lost his own ancestral home to a bank auction in the middle of this — died of a sudden cardiac arrest. The matter still unresolved.

We were a family of nine. We are eight.

Where it stands

I filed my rejoinder before the RBI Appellate Authority on 31.07.2026. I wrote again a month after the hearing.

No order. No acknowledgement. Silence.

I'm not asking anyone to take my word. Every line above is on the record — in the banks' own written admissions, in RBI's own complaint database, in IBBI's own confirmation letter.

I'm asking one question:

If a bank can manufacture a ₹34 crore liability against a citizen who never signed anything, hide the evidence from a criminal court, and face no consequence across 100 complaints and 3 years — what protects any of us?

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.
